extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Our dataset contains photos of 91 objects types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old. With a total of 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images, the creation of our dataset drew upon extensive crowd worker involvement via novel user interfaces for category detection, instance spotting and instance segmentation.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár. Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV] 21 Feb 2015.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created using a novel pipeline for gathering data with extensive use of Amazon Mechanical Turk. The process involved harvesting a large set of images containing contextual relationships and non-iconic object views by querying for pairs of objects in conjunction with scene-based queries. Each image was then labeled for object categories using a hierarchical approach, followed by labeling and verification of individual object instances, and finally instance segmentation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For images containing more than 10-15 instances of a given category, the remaining instances were marked as “crowds” using a single segment, and these areas are ignored for evaluation. Additionally, 11 categories (hat, shoe, eyeglasses, mirror, window, door, street sign, plate, desk, blender, hair brush) were not collected for segmentations in the 2014 release due to reasons like too many instances, ambiguity, confusion with other categories, or too few instances.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from Flickr and by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., “dog + car”) and scene/object category pairs.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, and the second half will be released in 2015.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed across dataset splits using [43]. Images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates. An explicit filtering stage was performed to remove iconic images when searching for single categories.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk using a three-stage pipeline: 1) Category Labeling: Workers used a hierarchical approach, dragging and dropping category icons onto one instance per super-category. 8 workers labeled each image to ensure high recall. 2) Instance Spotting: For each identified category, 8 workers placed a cross on up to 10 instances per category per image. A magnifying glass feature aided in finding small instances. 3) Instance Segmentation: A single worker segmented each object instance using a modified OpenSurfaces interface. Workers completed a training task to ensure quality. A verification step involved 3 to 5 workers judging each segmentation, with insufficient quality segmentations discarded and re-added to the pool. For dense instances (more than 10-15), 'crowd labeling' was used where workers painted all pixels belonging to the category.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). The user interface for instance segmentation was modified from the OpenSurfaces project [16].
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Crowd worker quality for category labeling was analyzed by comparing precision and recall against seven expert workers (co-authors), with ground truth determined by majority expert vote. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any expert. Worker precision and recall were also re-examined on a larger set of images using a leave-one-out evaluation, showing that workers completing more jobs had higher precision, and work from low-precision workers was rejected. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators; if any indicated it was bad, 2 more workers reviewed it. Segmentations not receiving at least 4 out of 5 favorable votes were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For category labeling, 8 workers labeled each image. For instance spotting, 8 workers labeled each image. For instance segmentation, a single worker segmented each instance. For segmentation verification, 3 to 5 workers judged each segmentation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is planned for a split release: the first half in 2014 and the second half in 2015. MS COCO will evolve and grow over time, with up-to-date information available online, implying ongoing maintenance.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes a 'person' category, but no explicit sensitive human attributes (e.g., gender, socio-economic status, geography, language, age, culture, experience) are mentioned as collected.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset aims to reduce bias towards 'iconic' object views by focusing on 'non-iconic' images and objects in natural contexts. However, the selection process removed categories difficult to obtain with many instances (greater than 5,000), potentially biasing towards common objects. The dataset also explicitly only includes 'thing' categories, not 'stuff', which is a design choice but limits the scope.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently only labels 'things' and not 'stuff' categories, which could provide significant contextual information. It lacks additional annotations such as object occlusion levels or keypoints, which could benefit many object detection algorithms. The 2014 release was limited to 80 categories, omitting 11 categories due to reasons like too many instances, ambiguity, confusion with other categories, or too few instances. For dense object instances, individual segmentations are not provided beyond 10-15 instances, with remaining instances marked as 'crowds' and ignored for evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition, particularly for detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. It is intended for training, testing, and validation of machine learning algorithms, with specific splits provided for these purposes (training, validation, and testing images).
